output:
To: docs/climate-programme/border-revenues-launch/handover
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Handover — Thursday launch (draft, read this first)

Inês,

I'm sorry to do this to you in a note. My father is ill and I am with my family. I'm on the train tonight and I don't know yet how long I'll be away, which means Thursday is yours. I won't pretend I've left things tidy: I found the figure 3 error at four this afternoon and I've been packing ever since.

Before anything else, the thing I want you to hear from me directly: you know this paper as well as I do. You ran the annex B sensitivity runs yourself. I'm not handing this over because I think it will hold up in spite of you — I'm handing it over because I know it will hold up with you. And I am sorry to drop it on you this way.

If you only have time for three things, make them these: Hanna and the press release, slides 6 and 9, and the badge names to Tomás by Wednesday noon. Everything below that is detail.

**1. The number — tonight or first thing tomorrow**

Figure 3 and the summary were built on the old 2030 revenue estimate; the free allocation phase-out wasn't applied. The correct figure for 2030 LDC-relevant revenue is EUR 1.4 billion, not EUR 2.1 billion. The conclusion of the paper does not change. The headline number does.

- PDF v7 on the drive is already corrected — pages 3, 14 and 15. That's the version that goes out. Check that nobody circulates v6, and search the deck and anything else we're handing out for "2.1" in case it's in a place I haven't looked.
- Deck v4 is not corrected. Slides 6 and 9. My speaker notes are still in it; I don't think I wrote the old number in them but I wouldn't bet the launch on it.
- The embargoed press release Hanna sent on Friday says 2.1. That's the one that worries me most.
- If anyone asks who made the mistake: I did, not you. Say so plainly and move on. There's no version of this where you take the blame for my error, and I'd rather you didn't soften it either.

**2. Hanna and the press release**

Thirty-four Brussels contacts have the wrong number sitting in their inboxes under embargo until Thursday 10:00. Hanna needs to send a corrected release to the same list before then — tomorrow if she can, Wednesday at the latest, so it's at the top of their inboxes rather than buried.

Two things to tell her: the number is 1.4, and the conclusion is unchanged so the framing of the release stands as written. If she needs a senior name to sign off a corrected version, Geert knows I'm away and can do it — ask him directly, don't wait to see whether he offers.

Hanna also lined up two background calls for Wednesday, 14:00 and 15:00, and told the journalists I'd be available. Either take them or ask her to move them — decide tomorrow morning so she has room to manoeuvre. If you take them, the only things that matter are 1.4 and "conclusion unchanged". You don't need to defend the whole paper on a twenty-minute phone call, and you shouldn't try to.

**3. Slides and the new timings**

Tomás emailed this morning with a change. Lindqvist has a vote moved into Thursday lunchtime and has to leave at 13:30. The presentation is 15 minutes instead of 20, and the panel starts at 12:50. She wants to take at least two questions herself before she goes. So cut the deck to 15 minutes, protect the revenue slide, and make sure there's a clean handover into questions well before 13:30. Worth a short call with Tomás about how he wants the chair handled once she's gone — the run of show still has Q&A at 13:40, which now sits awkwardly after her departure.

Badges: Tomás needs the final names from our side by Wednesday 12:00, or security won't let people in. This is the kind of thing that quietly goes wrong. Send him whatever list you have and copy the office so someone else is holding it too.

**4. Kessler**

He will come at you on the 80% pass-through. That's his line, and he'll try to use it in the first two minutes to set the tone for the whole panel. Don't let him. The answer, said openly and without defensiveness: 80% is the central case; annex B runs the sensitivity at 40% and 60%; the result holds at 60% and weakens at 40%. Give it as a range we tested, not as a concession. On resource shuffling, we agree it's a real risk — section 5.2 — and we recommend the Commission's monitoring report.

Abena will very likely back you on the LDC side. She was strong on the call and she's remote; the link is in the calendar invite and she tested it last week, so it works.

**5. The room**

You are better live than you think you are. In Lisbon, when the projector died in the middle of the panel, you didn't pause, you didn't apologise, you just kept going and carried the whole thing. That's the person who should be at the podium on Thursday, not me reading from notes. Lindqvist is friendly, Abena is on your side, and half the room will be thinking about lunch by 13:00.

**6. After the event**

Lucy Tran from the Halvorsen Foundation will be there with a colleague. She needs two photos and the attendance numbers for their grant report by 4 December. Nothing to do on the day beyond asking Tomás for the count and getting someone to take the photos — but put it in your calendar now, because it will otherwise surface in three weeks.

**What you don't need to do**

Don't redo the analysis. Don't rewrite the paper. Don't rebuild the deck from scratch. The conclusion stands, the correction is narrow, and the version on the drive is already right.

You can call me. After 9 tomorrow morning I may not pick up, but I'll call back when I can, and I'll read this on the train before it goes anywhere — so if something here is wrong or already out of date, that's on me too.

Thank you. I mean it.

Marieke
